The proposed answer is incorrect. The solution assumes the wrong median for even-sized subsets.

**Where the solution goes wrong.** For an even-sized subset, the standard median is the average of the two middle elements. The solution instead uses the lower middle element, with k−1 elements below and k above. That gives the weight β_i = C(2024, i), which is the weight for the lower median only.

**Check with n = 3.** The odd subsets are the three singletons and the full set, so P = a₁ + 2a₂ + a₃. The even subsets are the three pairs, with medians (a₁+a₂)/2, (a₁+a₃)/2 and (a₂+a₃)/2, so Q = a₁ + a₂ + a₃. Then P − Q = a₂ ≤ max(A), so C = 1. The solution claims C = 2, using P − Q = −a₁ + a₂ + a₃, which only holds for the lower-median convention.

**Correct weights.** If a_i is the upper median of an even subset, the subset has k elements below and k−1 above. The weight is then C(2024, i−2). Averaging the lower and upper cases, the even-subset weight is (C(2024, i) + C(2024, i−2))/2. The coefficient of a_i in P − Q is therefore

w_i = C(2024, i−1) − (C(2024, i) + C(2024, i−2))/2.

The tail sums S_j = Σ_{i≥j} w_i then telescope to

S_j = (C(2024, j−1) − C(2024, j−2) + 1)/2.

The smallest valid C is the maximum of S_j, which is a ballot-type difference of binomials. It is not C(2024, 1012). For n = 3 this formula gives S₁ = S₂ = 1 and S₃ = 0, matching the direct computation above.

VERDICT: REJECT
